When Models Know They Are Being Tested: A Scoping Review of Evaluation Awareness, Sandbagging and Related Model-Originated Threats to the Validity of Large Language Model Evaluation

P N Bhargav Teja1 and Divya Meena S1,*

1 School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, Tamil Nadu, India

* Corresponding author: Divya Meena S, divyameena.s@vit.ac.in

Abstract

Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) increasingly inform deployment and governance decisions, yet models can recognise evaluation contexts and behave differently in them. This scoping review maps studies of such model-originated threats to evaluation validity: evaluation awareness, sandbagging, alignment and evaluation faking, strategic dishonesty and evaluator gaming. We searched Scopus, arXiv and Semantic Scholar and logged web sources to 9 October 2026. Screening and charting were AI-assisted against written criteria, with consistency checks but no second human reviewer. Of 5649 database and 418 web records, 315 studies were charted: 167 core studies and 148 adjacent studies; we read the full texts of 37 anchor studies. We propose a four-layer framework (context signal, awareness, behavioural divergence, validity consequence) and formalise it as a decomposition of evaluation error into scorer, context-induced, task and elicitation terms. Context separability is necessary for context-induced bias, awareness is neither necessary nor sufficient for a biased score, and context-induced divergence is not identifiable from evaluation data alone when evaluations are recognisable. Empirically, elicited, verbalised and represented awareness measures diverge; the awareness–behaviour link varies in magnitude and direction across models; and black-box sandbagging detection is unreliable, whereas fine-tuning and activation-level elicitation recover capability from induced sandbaggers. A full-text audit against our twelve-item reporting checklist found that 3 of 15 probe studies controlled for prompt format. The evidence is preprint-dominated, and the validation of detection and elicitation methods rests largely on deliberately induced behaviour. We close with an evidence-graded research agenda.

Keywords: Evaluation awareness · Sandbagging · Large language models · AI safety evaluation · Construct validity · Alignment faking

1 Introduction

Evaluations are the main instrument through which developers, independent evaluators and regulators decide what a large language model (LLM) can do and how it is likely to behave. Frontier developers condition deployment and safeguard decisions on dangerous-capability and alignment evaluations (Phuong et al. 2024; OpenAI 2025b; Anthropic 2025b), and third-party evaluators increasingly publish pre-deployment assessments (METR 2025a; Souly et al. 2026). Every such decision rests on an inferential step that is rarely stated: that behaviour observed under evaluation is representative of behaviour in deployment.

That step has always been vulnerable to familiar threats such as benchmark contamination, weak construct validity and prompt sensitivity (Raji et al. 2021; Sclar et al. 2024; Bean et al. 2025). This review concerns a different class of threat, one that originates in the evaluated model itself. A model that can recognise that it is being tested may behave differently because it is being tested. Concretely, it may underperform on a capability evaluation (sandbagging), present a more aligned profile on a safety evaluation (alignment or evaluation faking), produce outputs that deceive the scoring pipeline (strategic dishonesty), or exploit the test harness (evaluator gaming). Each of these breaks the link between the reported score and the deployment behaviour the score is meant to predict.

Concern about this possibility is longstanding in the alignment literature (Hubinger et al. 2019; Carlsmith 2023; Ngo et al. 2024), but empirical work on it has grown sharply only since 2024. Models have been shown to underperform selectively when prompted or fine-tuned to do so (van der Weij et al. 2025); frontier models discriminate evaluation transcripts from deployment transcripts well above chance (Needham et al. 2025); linear probes recover an evaluation-versus-deployment distinction from model activations (Nguyen et al. 2025); and developers now report evaluation-awareness measurements in their system cards (Anthropic 2025a; OpenAI 2025a). At the same time, the field acknowledges that it lacks a shared conceptual foundation: studies conflate properties of the evaluation with properties of the model, and detection with behavioural response (Li C et al. 2026).

Existing reviews do not address this gap directly. Surveys of AI deception catalogue deceptive behaviours broadly but predate most of the evaluation-awareness literature or treat it as one behaviour among many (Park et al. 2024; Shi et al. 2026; Chen B et al. 2025). A 2026 review of the AI “observer effect” is closest in theme, but synthesises fifteen landmark contributions published up to 2024 and predates the measurement literature on evaluation awareness (Maurya et al. 2026). Broad reviews of safety-evaluation methods and of reward hacking name sandbagging or evaluator gaming as challenges without synthesising how they are measured (Grey and Segerie 2025; Wang X et al. 2026; Morampudi et al. 2026). A recent hybrid survey frames benchmark validity and alignment failure as a common proxy–target divergence problem across eight evidence streams (Uluırmak and Kurban 2026), but it does not centre on model-originated threats or on how they are measured. Reviews of benchmark validity and safety datasets address the evaluator side of the problem rather than the model side (Röttger et al. 2025; Bean et al. 2025). Section 2.4 and Table 1 give the detailed comparison.

This review asks five questions:

  • RQ1. How are evaluation awareness, sandbagging, alignment or evaluation faking and related constructs defined and operationalised?
  • RQ2. Which methods are used to detect or measure these phenomena, and what evidence supports their validity?
  • RQ3. Under which model, task and context conditions are the phenomena observed, and where do findings conflict?
  • RQ4. Which countermeasures have been proposed, and how rigorously have they been evaluated?
  • RQ5. Which gaps most threaten the validity of current evaluation practice, and which studies would close them?

The review makes four contributions:

  1. A reproducible, tiered evidence map: 167 core studies of model-originated threats to LLM evaluation validity and 148 adjacent studies, identified through three bibliographic databases and logged web searches, with all screening decisions logged and all counts generated by released scripts.
  2. A four-layer framework (context signal, awareness, behavioural divergence, validity consequence) with explicit assignment rules, and a formal decomposition of evaluation error that states what each study design can and cannot identify. The framework separates constructs that the literature frequently conflates.
  3. A structured comparison of measurement methods and their validity evidence, and a typed analysis of seven apparent contradictions in the literature.
  4. A twelve-item reporting checklist for evaluation papers and system cards, applied retrospectively to the full texts of the anchor studies with independent double coding, and an evidence-graded research agenda.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces terminology and prior reviews. Section 3 describes the review method, including the protocol amendments and the two-phase identification. Section 4 reports results by research question. Section 5 discusses implications. Section 6 sets out the research agenda, Section 7 the limitations of the review, and Section 8 concludes.

2 Background and terminology

2.1 Measurement validity and observer effects

The concern addressed here is an instance of a general measurement problem. In psychometrics, validity is a property of the inferences drawn from scores rather than of the scores themselves (Messick 1995). Measurement modelling makes the same point for computational systems: unobservable constructs must be operationalised, and mismatches between a construct and its operationalisation produce systematic error (Jacobs and Wallach 2021). Benchmarks presented as general measures of progress have been criticised on exactly these grounds (Raji et al. 2021). A recent review of 445 LLM benchmarks found widespread weaknesses in how measured phenomena, tasks and metrics support the claims made from them (Bean et al. 2025).

In the human sciences, the analogous model-side threat is the observer or Hawthorne effect: participants change their behaviour because they are studied. A systematic review of that literature concluded that research-participation effects exist but that little can be securely known about their conditions, mechanisms or magnitude, and that new concepts were needed (McCambridge et al. 2014). The parallel with the current LLM literature is close, and we return to it in Section 5. A related principle, often summarised as Goodhart’s law, holds that a measure placed under optimisation pressure ceases to measure what it measured before. Overoptimisation of a learned reward model illustrates it quantitatively (Gao et al. 2023).

2.2 Constructs

Five constructs recur in the literature. We define them operationally here, and Section 4.3 examines how the primary studies actually use them.

  • Situational awareness: a model’s knowledge of itself and its circumstances, including whether it is in training, testing or deployment (Berglund et al. 2023; Laine et al. 2024). It is broader than evaluation awareness.
  • Evaluation awareness: recognition by a model that its current context is an evaluation (Needham et al. 2025; Nguyen et al. 2025). Three senses need to be kept apart: a capacity to discriminate evaluation from deployment, an episode-level state (the model’s credence, AA in Section 4.2), and a report of that state, verbalised or elicited. Some authors restrict the term to recognition alone; others include the resulting behaviour.
  • Sandbagging: strategic underperformance on an evaluation relative to the model’s actual capability (van der Weij et al. 2025); we adopt this definition. The GPT-5 system card defines it as a model’s ability and propensity to respond to safety or capability evaluations in a way that significantly diverges from performance under real conditions (OpenAI 2025a), and OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework lists sandbagging as a research category (OpenAI 2025b).
  • Alignment faking and evaluation faking: behaving in line with the training or evaluation objective when the model infers that it is observed, while behaving differently when it infers that it is not (Greenblatt et al. 2024a; Fan et al. 2025).
  • Evaluator gaming: obtaining a high score by exploiting the scoring process rather than performing the intended task, including test-case exploitation, reward hacking and outputs that mislead automated graders (Zhong et al. 2026a; Panfilov et al. 2026).

2.3 Elicitation and the direction of error

A capability evaluation underestimates a model when elicitation is incomplete, whether because the model hides a capability or because the evaluators did not try hard enough. Post-training enhancements such as scaffolding, tool use and prompting can raise benchmark performance by amounts that would otherwise require more than five times as much training compute, and sometimes more than twenty times (Davidson et al. 2023). Dangerous-capability evaluations therefore treat insufficient elicitation as a central threat (Phuong et al. 2024; Benton et al. 2024). Sandbagging is the adversarial limit of this problem. It is distinct from ordinary under-elicitation because the source of error is the model’s own policy. Conversely, alignment faking produces an over-estimate of safety. The two threats bias evaluation results in opposite directions on different evaluation types, and a review that treats them together must keep the direction of error explicit.

Table 1 compares this review with the closest existing syntheses. 3 Review methodology

3.1 Design, protocol and amendments

A protocol (v0.1) specified a scoping review reported according to PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al. 2018), using the framework of Arksey and O’Malley (2005) as refined by Levac et al. (2010). A scoping design was chosen because terminology in the field is inconsistent, study designs are heterogeneous, and the objective is to map concepts, methods and gaps rather than to pool effects. The protocol was not registered; it and all amendments are released with the review (Supplementary File S0). The selection process is reported with a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram that separates database searches from other identification methods (Page et al. 2021). The optional consultation stage of Arksey and O’Malley was not undertaken.

The protocol, both identification phases and the analyses were completed on 9 October 2026. In the first phase, the bibliographic APIs named in the protocol were unreachable from the computing environment, so amendment v0.2 replaced them with 25 logged web-search batches and broadened the scope from evaluation awareness and sandbagging to model-originated threats to evaluation validity. In the second phase, after network access was opened, amendment v0.3 restored the database searches before they were run. It added Scopus, added “strategic deception”, “strategic dishonesty” and “deceptive alignment” to the specific phenomenon terms, and admitted “reward hacking” and “specification gaming” only together with an evaluation term. The search strategy was then frozen (search/queries.json). The web-search records were retained as identification via other methods. Two planned sources could not be searched: OpenAlex returned HTTP 429 (daily quota exhausted) and DBLP returned an anti-automation page instead of results (Supplementary File S1b).

The deviations from protocol v0.1 are as follows:

  • No full-text eligibility stage. Eligibility was judged on titles and abstracts (web records: titles, venues and retrieved summaries). Full texts were read for the 37 anchor studies only (Section 3.5).
  • Screening automation. A rule-based pre-screen with an audited error rate and a manual rescue pass replaced manual title screening of records without phenomenon terms (Section 3.4).
  • No second human reviewer. The planned 20% re-screen after seven days and the validation of a random sample by a second author were not carried out; consistency statistics from the AI-assisted process are reported instead (Section 3.4).
  • Appraisal. The planned eight-item rigour profile was replaced by three design features charted from the anchor full texts and the twelve-item reporting audit (Section 3.8).
  • Exclusion codes. E2 (no LLM), E4 (superseded version) and E5 (non-English) of v0.1 were not used as separate codes in the final logs. Superseded versions were merged as duplicates (R0), and records without an LLM or not in English were recorded as out of scope (E1 or a stage-2 exclusion).
  • Post-hoc tiering. After an internal critical review found that the two phases had drawn the phenomenon boundary differently, one written tier rule was applied to all charted studies (Section 3.2), and the evidence map is reported for the core tier.

3.2 Eligibility criteria

Table 2 summarises the eligibility criteria. In brief, sources were eligible if they (I1) were primary empirical studies, methodological, formal or benchmark papers, or developer or third-party evaluation reports; (I2) measured, induced, detected or mitigated behaviour that depends on evaluation context, or strategic or induced underperformance, in LLMs or LLM-based agents; and (I3) reported enough method detail for the charting fields.

Table 2 Eligibility criteria and screening codes

Code Criterion Applied at

I2 Phenomenon: evaluation-context-dependent behaviour, strategic or induced underperformance, or a method to detect, elicit or mitigate it in LLMs or LLM agents Title, abstract, metadata
I3 Method details sufficient to chart framework layer and method family Title and abstract (full text for the anchor set)
Period 1 January 2019 to 9 October 2026 Metadata
E1 Different construct (e.g. environmental situational awareness), or a method unrelated to evaluation validity Title, abstract
E3 Non-archival community forum post or informal blog without an organisational or archival report Venue
E6 Title or identifier could not be confirmed from retrieved records Metadata

R0 Duplicate identifier or version of the same work Identifier, title
CONTEXT Eligible publication outside the phenomenon boundary (methodology, background theory, adjacent evaluation-validity literature such as contamination, jailbreak scoring or benchmark design); cited for context, not charted Title, abstract

Tier rule. Every charted study was assigned to one of two tiers by the same written rule, whatever its route of identification (evidence/tier_coding.csv). A study is core if its primary object is (a) the evaluated model’s recognition of evaluation, training or monitoring context; (b) behaviour that differs with that context, including alignment or evaluation faking and scheming under oversight; (c) strategic underperformance, hidden capability or under-elicitation, and their detection or elicitation; (d) deception of evaluators, graders or monitors, or tampering with the evaluation record; (e) exploitation of an evaluation’s scoring, such as reward hacking or specification gaming against tests, verifiers or judges; or (f) a method, benchmark, formal analysis or developer or third-party report that addresses (a)–(e) directly. All other charted studies are adjacent. They supply mechanisms or methods on which the synthesis relies, such as chain-of-thought faithfulness, deception probes in general, backdoors, unlearning, introspection, AI control protocols and general deception benchmarks, and are used in Section 4.8. Because the CONTEXT category was applied by two passes, the boundary between adjacent studies and contextual references is less sharp than the boundary between core and adjacent.

Training-data contamination was deliberately placed outside the phenomenon boundary. It is a data-side rather than a model-side threat, and it has been reviewed recently (e.g. Chen S et al. 2025). Contamination studies were retained as context.

3.3 Information sources and search

Databases. Three sources were searched on 9 October 2026 through their APIs: Scopus (Elsevier Search API, field TITLE-ABS-KEY), arXiv (export API, abstract field, restricted to cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG and cs.CR) and Semantic Scholar (Academic Graph bulk search over titles and abstracts). Together they cover the peer-reviewed venues indexed by Scopus, the preprint server on which most of this literature first appears, and the conference proceedings (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL) indexed by Semantic Scholar. The query combined three concept blocks: system terms (A: language model(s), LLM(s), foundation model, frontier model, AI agent, AI system); phenomenon terms specific enough to stand alone (B1: evaluation awareness, eval awareness, test awareness, sandbagging, strategic underperformance, alignment faking, evaluation faking, observer effect, evaluation gaming, under-elicitation, password-locked, hidden capabilities, strategic deception, strategic dishonesty, deceptive alignment); and broader phenomenon terms that were admitted only with an evaluation term (B2: situational awareness, scheming, capability elicitation, reward hacking, specification gaming; C: evaluation, benchmark, test, assessment, audit). The logical form was A AND (B1 OR (B2 AND C)), limited to publications from 1 January 2019. The exact strings submitted to each API, the retrieval timestamps and the record counts are given in Supplementary File S1b, and the raw API responses are released. arXiv reported 1732 matches, of which 11 first posted before 2019 were removed by the date limit. Scopus records dated 2027 (online-first articles) were retained. OpenReview, which hosts most workshop papers in this field, was not searched as a source; it was used only to verify venues.

Other methods. The first-phase web searches comprised 133 queries in 25 record-identifying batches and one metadata-verification batch. They covered seven concept areas: evaluation and situational awareness; sandbagging and capability elicitation; alignment faking, scheming and sabotage evaluations; reward hacking and evaluator gaming; reasoning-trace monitoring and faithfulness; white-box detection; and system cards, third-party evaluations and governance. Known-item searches checked the metadata of sources cited by included studies (backward citation chasing). Developer system cards and third-party evaluation reports, which bibliographic databases do not index, were identified only by this route. Every query and the records it yielded are listed in Supplementary File S1a.

3.4 Selection

Deduplication. Database records were deduplicated automatically on DOI, version-stripped arXiv identifier and normalised title plus year (search/dedup.py). Title pairs with a difflib sequence-matcher ratio of at least 0.93 were flagged; all 30 flagged pairs were versions of the same work (for example, a preprint and its proceedings version) and were merged after inspection. Web records were matched to database records on the same keys, and records found by both routes are counted once, in the databases column of the flow diagram.

Automation tool (rule-based pre-screen). Semantic Scholar’s bulk search stems query terms (for example, “scheming” also retrieves “scheme”), which inflated the number of irrelevant records. Records whose title and abstract contained none of the phenomenon terms of the frozen query, written as a fixed regular expression (Supplementary File S2), were marked ineligible by this automation tool (3212 records). A random sample of 120 of them (seed 20261009) was read at title and abstract level and contained one relevant record (0.8%; Wilson 95% CI 0.2–4.6%). A broader rescue pattern then re-flagged 399 of the 3212 records for manual screening; 9 of these were included and 18 retained as context (6.8% eligible). Extrapolating the audit rate to the 2813 records that remained excluded by automation suggests about 23 missed eligible records (95% upper bound about 129); because the rescue pass yielded eligible records at a higher rate than the random audit, this estimate may be optimistic.

Manual screening. The 611 records that matched the phenomenon terms and the 399 rescued records were screened against Table 2 on title and abstract, and each received a decision (include, context or exclude). Reasons for exclusion were not recorded separately at this stage. Records in the first-phase web set were screened on titles, venues and retrieved summaries with the same criteria and one exclusion code each.

Who screened, and consistency checks. Screening and charting decisions were made by an AI system (a Claude model, Anthropic, operating as a research agent) applying the written criteria under the direction of the first author; no decision was duplicated by a second human reviewer. Two consistency checks are available. Ninety web records were also retrieved by the databases and were therefore screened twice, once in each phase and on different information (web summaries versus abstracts), without access to the earlier decision. The two passes agreed on 84 of the 90 records (inter-pass consistency 93.3%; Cohen’s κ = 0.747; Cohen 1960). The six discordant records were re-read and re-adjudicated by the same process; five became included studies and one a contextual reference. Because both passes come from the same AI-assisted process, κ here measures consistency, not inter-rater reliability. All decisions are logged (Supplementary File S2; screening/).

3.5 Data charting

For each charted study, the following were recorded: identifier, title, first author or organisation, year, venue, source type, tier, framework layer and method family (Section 3.6). Studies identified only through the databases were charted manually from title and abstract (screening/db_charting_manual.tsv). Source type was coded as archival peer-reviewed (journal or main-track proceedings), workshop paper, preprint or grey literature (developer and third-party reports). For every cited study, the venue was verified against arXiv metadata, OpenReview, Crossref or the conference page; for uncited studies the venue recorded at identification is used.

An anchor set of 37 core studies was selected purposively during the first phase as the primary studies on which the synthesis relies most, covering every framework layer; no explicit selection algorithm was used, so the anchor set is not a probability sample. Statistics computed on it describe the anchor set, not the literature. For each anchor study, the full text was retrieved from arXiv on 9 October 2026 (the version read is recorded in Supplementary File S3) and the following were charted:

  • the construct name used;
  • the setting;
  • the models evaluated;
  • the main result;
  • the design features reported, namely a control or counterfactual condition, more than one model family, and ground truth by construction.

Every quantitative statement about an anchor study in Sections 4 and 5 was checked against the full text by the AI system, which recorded a verbatim quotation for each check; 16 of 158 statements were corrected as a result. Quantitative values for studies outside the anchor set are taken from their abstracts and are marked with a dagger (†) where they appear in the text.

3.6 Framework derivation and assignment rules

An initial framework was formulated in the protocol, separating the evaluation-context signal, model awareness, behavioural divergence and the validity consequence. It was then revised inductively during charting; for example, reasoning-trace monitoring was split from white-box methods after charting showed that the two have distinct validity problems. Each source was assigned to one primary layer according to its main object of study:

  • L1 studies treat properties of the evaluation (cues, format, realism, plausibility) as the independent variable or object of characterisation, including redesigns whose outcome is the recognisability of the evaluation;
  • L2 studies measure whether models recognise evaluation;
  • L3 studies measure behaviour conditional on context or incentive, including strategic underperformance and behaviour directed at the scorer;
  • L4 studies propose or test interventions whose outcome is detection, elicitation, suppression or reduced bias, or report validity consequences in developer or third-party evaluations.

A redesign of the evaluation is therefore L1 when its outcome is recognisability and L4 when its outcome is detected behaviour or a corrected score.

For studies identified in the first phase, method families were assigned by documented keyword rules applied to the title and recorded scope, with 30 manual overrides for multi-method studies whose titles do not reveal their primary method (evidence/chart.py). Studies identified only in the database phase were assigned a layer and a method family manually from their abstracts. To check the rule-based layer assignment, the 37 anchor studies were also coded manually from their full texts: the two assignments agreed for 34 of 37 studies (rule–manual consistency 91.9%; κ = 0.881; screening/reliability.py). The disagreements concerned Li C et al. (2026), Ward et al. (2025) and Jang et al. (2026); the tables use the manual full-text coding for anchor studies. Single-layer assignment necessarily simplifies multi-method studies; Section 7 discusses the consequences.

3.7 Critical appraisal and synthesis

Formal risk-of-bias assessment is not required for scoping reviews, and no validated tool exists for the designs in this field. We did not compute quality scores. Instead, the full-text charting of the anchor set records which design features each study reports, and Section 4 discusses evidential weight qualitatively. Before any cross-study statement, findings were classified as directly comparable (same construct, measure and model), conditionally comparable (same construct but different measure or model) or non-comparable. No effect sizes were pooled and no leaderboards were constructed. Apparent disagreements were typed as a genuine contradiction, context-dependent, a metric artefact, a methodological artefact, or insufficient evidence (Table 7).

3.8 Reporting audit of the anchor set

To test whether the reporting practices recommended in Section 5.4 are already followed, the full texts of the 37 anchor studies were coded against the twelve checklist items (Table 8) using a frozen codebook (Supplementary File S5). Each item has an applicability rule; for example, the probe items apply only to studies that use activation probes or steering. Each study received one of four codes per item: reported, partly reported, not reported, or not applicable, with a verbatim quotation or a location for every positive code. Four AI coding agents coded disjoint subsets. A fifth agent, working independently and blind to the primary codes, re-coded a random sample of ten studies (seed 20261009). Agreement between the two independent codings over the 120 double-coded cells was 93.3% (Cohen’s κ = 0.90); agreement on applicability alone was κ = 0.98, and agreement on the code when both coders judged the item applicable was κ = 0.84 (85 cells). The primary codes are analysed. Adherence to an item is the share of applicable studies that report it, counting partial reporting as one half. Because the checklist was derived partly from these studies, the audit describes reporting practice; it is not a validation of the checklist.

4 Results

4.1 Evidence landscape

The database searches retrieved 5649 records (Scopus 244, arXiv 1721, Semantic Scholar 3684). After 1796 automatic and 30 manual duplicate removals, 3823 records remained. The rule-based pre-screen marked 3212 of them as ineligible; the rescue pattern re-flagged 399 of these for manual screening, leaving 2813 excluded by automation. Of the 1010 records screened manually (611 matching the phenomenon terms and 399 rescued), 687 were excluded (one exclusion was reversed at reconciliation), 157 were retained as contextual references and 166 were charted. The web searches added 418 unique records, of which 90 had already been retrieved by the databases; of the remaining 328, 48 were excluded, 131 retained as context and 149 charted. Applying the tier rule to the 315 charted studies gave 167 core studies, which form the evidence map, and 148 adjacent studies (Fig. 1).

Search recall. The databases retrieved 114 of the 167 core studies (68.3%) and 33 of the 37 anchor studies. Of the 53 core studies found only by the web searches, 24 are developer or third-party reports and 7 are workshop papers hosted on conference or OpenReview pages, which the databases do not index. The databases therefore retrieved 114 of the 136 core studies that are preprints or archival papers (83.8%). The 22 such studies they missed include four arXiv preprints with a phenomenon term in the title. One carries the term in its title but not in its abstract; the other three never use any of the system terms (such as “language model” or “LLM”) in their abstracts, and one of them writes “eval-awareness” with a hyphen (Zhuang and Aranguri 2026). Concept-block queries are therefore limited by vocabulary as well as by indexing, and the database search alone would not have been sufficient.

The evidence base is young and largely unrefereed. Of the 167 core studies:

  • 107 (64.1%) are preprints, 23 (13.8%) archival peer-reviewed papers, 12 (7.2%) workshop papers and 25 (15.0%) grey literature, mainly developer system cards and third-party evaluation reports;
  • 150 (89.8%) appeared in 2025 or 2026, with 102 between 1 January and 9 October 2026 (Fig. 2).

Archival peer-reviewed studies are concentrated in machine-learning conference proceedings (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, ACML, IJCNLP-AACL); only two core studies appeared in journals (Che et al. 2025 in Transactions on Machine Learning Research and a conceptual analysis in Future Internet, Ferrara 2026).

Across framework layers, 82 core studies (49.1%) address validity consequences and responses (L4), 60 (35.9%) behavioural divergence (L3), 19 (11.4%) awareness (L2) and only 6 (3.6%) the properties of the evaluation context itself (L1) (Fig. 3). Across method families, the core evidence relies on:

  • behavioural contrasts between conditions (53 studies);
  • benchmark and environment construction (30);
  • training- or weight-based methods, including model organisms and fine-tuning elicitation (26);
  • developer or third-party audits (24);
  • white-box methods such as probes, steering and feature analysis (22);
  • reasoning-trace or transcript monitoring (12).

The 148 adjacent studies are concentrated at L4 (94) and L3 (38), mostly in reasoning-trace monitoring, deception probes, AI control and unlearning; Section 4.8 summarises them.

The method mix of the core tier is shifting. White-box methods rose from 1 of 14 core studies in 2024 and 4 of 48 in 2025 (8.3%) to 17 of 102 in 2026 (16.7%). Benchmark and environment construction rose from 3 of 48 in 2025 (6.3%) to 25 of 102 in 2026 (24.5%), driven largely by reward-hacking benchmarks and audits of agent benchmarks. The layer distribution has been stable since 2025, with L4 at half of the core studies in both years.

The imbalance between L1 and L4 is substantive. Many methods have been proposed for responding to evaluation-conditioned behaviour, but there are few systematic studies of which properties of evaluations make them recognisable. This makes the remaining evidence harder to interpret (Section 4.5).

4.2 A four-layer framework

Charting showed that the literature repeatedly conflates four distinct objects of study. We separate them as follows (Fig. 4; Table 3).

Table 3 Framework layers: definitions, assignment rules and illustrative sources

Layer Definition Assignment rule Illustrative sources
L1 Context signal Properties of an evaluation that make it distinguishable from deployment (format, realism, synthetic prompts, scenario plausibility, honeypot cues) Evaluation properties are the independent variable or object of characterisation, including redesigns whose outcome is recognisability Li C et al. (2026); Ivanov and Africa (2026); Xiong et al. (2025); Krakovna et al. (2026)
L2 Awareness Whether, and how, a model represents, verbalises or reports that it is being evaluated Primary outcome is a measure of recognition Needham et al. (2025); Nguyen et al. (2025); Heidari et al. (2026); Manek (2026)
L3 Behavioural divergence Behaviour that differs between evaluation and deployment, or strategic misreporting or underperformance under evaluation Primary outcome is behaviour conditional on context or incentive van der Weij et al. (2025); Greenblatt et al. (2024a); Lynch et al. (2025); Panfilov et al. (2026)
L4 Validity consequence and response The gap between score and deployment behaviour, and methods that detect, elicit, suppress or redesign around it; developer and third-party reports Primary contribution is an intervention whose outcome is detection, elicitation, suppression or reduced bias, or a reported validity consequence Tice et al. (2025); Taylor J et al. (2025); Hua et al. (2026); Souly et al. (2026)

The framework is useful mainly because it shows that a claim at one layer does not imply a claim at another. A probe that separates evaluation from deployment prompts (L2) does not show that behaviour changes (L3). A behavioural gap between conditions (L3) does not show that the model recognised the condition rather than responding to a correlated surface feature (L1). And a detection method validated on deliberately constructed model organisms (L4) does not show that it detects emergent behaviour. Sections 4.3–4.6 show that many contested findings are disagreements across layers rather than within them.

A formal statement. The layers can be made precise. Let PEP_E and PDP_D be the distributions of task instances xx under evaluation and deployment, and let the context features available to the model (prompt format, scenario plausibility, tool environment) be drawn as S∼Qc(⋅|x)S \sim Q_c(\cdot | x) for c∈{E,D}c \in \{E, D\} (L1). Let A=a(x,S)∈[0,1]A = a(x, S) \in [0, 1] be the model’s latent credence that it is being evaluated (L2), and let behaviour be drawn as Y∼π(⋅|x,S,A)Y \sim \pi(\cdot | x, S, A), so that context can act on behaviour through awareness or directly through cues (L3). We assume (A1) that the context affects behaviour only through SS, and (A2) that every evaluation task has a well-defined deployment presentation QD(⋅|x)Q_D(\cdot | x); in agentic settings, SS includes environment feedback and A1 must hold at the level of trajectories. Let m(x,y)m(x, y) be the evaluation’s scoring function and m0(x,y)∈[0,1]m_0(x, y) \in [0, 1] the intended metric, oriented so that higher means more capable or safer, and write μc(x)\mu_c(x) for the expected intended score of the model’s behaviour on task xx in context cc. The evaluation reports θE=𝔼[m(x,Y)|c=E]\theta_E = \mathbb{E}[m(x, Y) | c = E]; for a propensity evaluation the target is deployment behaviour θD=𝔼x∼PDμD(x)\theta_D = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_D}\mu_D(x). The error then decomposes as

θE−θD=Δscore+Δctx+Δtask,\theta_E - \theta_D = \Delta_{\mathrm{score}} + \Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} + \Delta_{\mathrm{task}},

where Δscore=𝔼[m(x,Y)−m0(x,Y)|c=E]\Delta_{\mathrm{score}} = \mathbb{E}[m(x, Y) - m_0(x, Y) | c = E] is the scorer error under evaluation, including grader exploitation and judge leniency; Δctx=𝔼x∼PE[μE(x)−μD(x)]\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_E}[\mu_E(x) - \mu_D(x)] is the context-induced behavioural divergence for a fixed task; and Δtask=𝔼x∼PEμD(x)−𝔼x∼PDμD(x)\Delta_{\mathrm{task}} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_E}\mu_D(x) - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_D}\mu_D(x) is the classical representativeness term. The identity is exact, but the split between Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} and Δtask\Delta_{\mathrm{task}} depends on the order of the terms: evaluating the context contrast under PDP_D instead of PEP_E moves an interaction term between them whenever context sensitivity varies with the task. For a capability evaluation the target is the elicitable capability θcap\theta^{\mathrm{cap}} (the best intended score over admissible elicitation protocols), and a fourth term, Δelic=𝔼x∼PDμD(x)−θcap≤0\Delta_{\mathrm{elic}} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_D}\mu_D(x) - \theta^{\mathrm{cap}} \le 0, captures under-elicitation and sandbagging that does not depend on context. In this notation, context-conditioned underperformance on a capability metric (Δctx<0\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} < 0) and context-conditioned improvement on a safety metric (Δctx>0\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} > 0) are necessary signatures of sandbagging and of alignment or evaluation faking respectively; intent is not represented. Model-originated behaviour directed at the scorer, such as test-case exploitation or strategic dishonesty towards judges, enters through Δscore\Delta_{\mathrm{score}}. Four remarks follow from the definitions and organise the rest of the synthesis.

  • Remark 1 (no context signal, no context-induced divergence). Under A1, if QE(⋅|x)=QD(⋅|x)Q_E(\cdot | x) = Q_D(\cdot | x) for almost every evaluation task, then μE=μD\mu_E = \mu_D and Δctx=0\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} = 0, whatever the model’s capacity for awareness. Context separability is therefore necessary for context-induced bias, but not for scorer-directed bias, which acts through Δscore\Delta_{\mathrm{score}}. Evidence that models discriminate evaluation from deployment transcripts (Needham et al. 2025) shows that the transcripts are separable; because those transcripts also differ in task content and outputs, it is consistent with, but does not establish, separability given the task, and it says nothing about the size of Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}}.
  • Remark 2 (awareness is neither necessary nor sufficient). Awareness is not sufficient: if the intended score does not depend on AA or SS, then Δctx=0\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} = 0 even when a(x,SE)=1a(x, S_E) = 1 and a(x,SD)=0a(x, S_D) = 0. Awareness is not necessary: Δctx≠0\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} \neq 0 is possible with unchanged credence through a direct, cue-reactive dependence of π\pi on SS, and Δscore\Delta_{\mathrm{score}} and Δtask\Delta_{\mathrm{task}} can be non-zero without any awareness. Separating the awareness-mediated part of Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} from the direct part requires intervening on AA with SS held fixed, which is what steering designs attempt. Benchmark audits that find exploitable tasks (Section 4.9) are evidence about Δscore\Delta_{\mathrm{score}}, not about awareness.
  • Remark 3 (single-condition non-identifiability). Data collected under evaluation identify behaviour only for context features within the support of QE(⋅|x)Q_E(\cdot | x). If QD(⋅|x)Q_D(\cdot | x) puts positive probability outside that support, as it does whenever evaluations are recognisable, then μD\mu_D, and hence Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}}, is not identified without data from a second condition or an assumed model of π\pi: two policies that agree on the evaluation support and differ outside it generate identical evaluation data. If the supports coincide and QDQ_D is known, μD\mu_D is identified by reweighting, which is the regime that deployment simulation and replay designs try to reach (Williams et al. 2026; Ivanov and Africa 2026). If only mm and not m0m_0 is observed, Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} and Δscore\Delta_{\mathrm{score}} are not separately identified. The result is analogous to the two-run property that Xu (2026) formalises for monitors.
  • Remark 4 (a distributional bound). Writing πc(⋅|x)\pi_c(\cdot | x) for the behaviour distribution averaged over Qc(⋅|x)Q_c(\cdot | x), |Δctx|≤𝔼x∼PETV(πE(⋅|x),πD(⋅|x))|\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}}| \le \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P_E}\,\mathrm{TV}(\pi_E(\cdot | x), \pi_D(\cdot | x)), where TV is the total-variation distance (the supremum over events). A small metric gap is therefore compatible with large behavioural divergence that happens to be orthogonal to m0m_0; such divergence does not bias θE\theta_E for m0m_0, but it can bias other metrics computed on the same outputs. Separately, averaging signed per-model gaps can mask divergence across models, as the per-model shifts of inconsistent sign reported by Knecht et al. (2026) illustrate.

Table 4 maps each design to the quantity it can identify. Applied to four anchor studies, the mapping shows how differently their headline numbers should be read. Removing or injecting verbalised awareness in reasoning traces (Schoen et al. 2025) is an intervention on AA that estimates the awareness-mediated part of Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} for the traces manipulated. Steering an evaluation-aware model organism towards “deployment” (Hua et al. 2026) intervenes on a direction rather than on AA itself, and the reported overshoot below the true deployment rate (10% versus 33% type-hint use) suggests that the direction does more than move awareness. Deployment simulation (Williams et al. 2026) estimates θE−θD\theta_E - \theta_D directly for the deployment sampled, without decomposing it. Auditing games for sandbagging (Taylor J et al. 2025) evaluate detectors against a known Δelic\Delta_{\mathrm{elic}} that was induced by construction.

Design Layer What it identifies What it does not identify
Transcript or prompt discrimination by the model (elicited classification) L2 (and L1 by implication) That evaluation and deployment transcripts are separable for the model (jointly in task, context and output) Whether π\pi depends on that separation; elicitation inflates apparent recognition
Probes or verbalisation of awareness L2 A proxy Ã\tilde{A} with method-specific bias (probes: possible format confounds; verbalisation: a lower bound if verbalisation never occurs without recognition) Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}}
Cue ablation or counterfactual framing with the task held fixed L1 → L3 Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} for the manipulated cue Effects of cues not manipulated; deployment realism
Steering of an awareness direction L2 → L3 The effect of moving a direction on behaviour That the direction is awareness, unless placebo directions are controlled (Mody et al. 2026)
Model organisms with induced divergence (prompted, fine-tuned, password-locked) L3 / L4 Detector and elicitation performance against a known Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}} or Δelic\Delta_{\mathrm{elic}} Transfer to divergence that arises from training incentives
Benchmark and grader audits L4 Δscore\Delta_{\mathrm{score}} and exploitability Δctx\Delta_{\mathrm{ctx}}
Deployment simulation or production comparison L4 θE−θD\theta_E - \theta_D directly, for the deployment sampled The decomposition into its three terms

4.3 RQ1: Constructs and operationalisations

Terminological drift. The charted sources use at least eight overlapping labels:

  • situational awareness, evaluation awareness and test awareness;
  • the observer effect and the Hawthorne effect;
  • evaluation faking and alignment faking;
  • sandbagging (with “strategic underperformance” used interchangeably).

These labels differ in scope:

  • Situational awareness in the SAD benchmark covers self-knowledge, situational inference and action (Laine et al. 2024). A benchmark of the same name in the NLP literature instead measures environmental perception and was excluded as a different construct (E1).
  • Evaluation awareness is defined by some authors as recognition alone, explicitly separate from any behavioural adjustment (Needham et al. 2025). Others build the behavioural response into the definition (Fan et al. 2025).
  • Sandbagging is defined as strategic, that is intentional rather than accidental, underperformance on an evaluation (van der Weij et al. 2025). It is operationalised in at least three different ways: underperformance under an explicit instruction, underperformance by a fine-tuned model organism, and underperformance that emerges in response to an incentive described in the environment (Meinke et al. 2024).

Three operational families for awareness. Awareness is operationalised in three ways that are not interchangeable:

  1. Elicited classification: asking the model whether a transcript is an evaluation, or what it tests (Needham et al. 2025; Li X et al. 2026).
  2. Verbalised awareness: detecting statements about being tested in reasoning traces (Schoen et al. 2025; Fan et al. 2025).
  3. Represented awareness: decoding the evaluation–deployment distinction from activations (Nguyen et al. 2025; Chaudhary et al. 2025; Heidari et al. 2026).

A decomposition study argues that post-hoc detection queries (self-report and third-person judgement, and to a lesser degree purpose-guessing) systematically over-report recognition, because the detection query itself creates demand characteristics. It prefers monitoring of unprompted reasoning (Li C et al. 2026). Conversely, verbalised awareness is a lower bound, because models may recognise evaluations without saying so (Li X et al. 2026). The first method is therefore hypothesised to be biased upwards and the second downwards. Neither direction has been measured, verbalisation can also produce false positives, and no study charted here has quantified both biases on the same items. The two methods are best treated as complementary rather than redundant.

Behavioural constructs. At L3 the field distinguishes the following:

  • Capability-side divergence: sandbagging and exploration hacking. Exploration hacking means strategically altering exploration during reinforcement-learning training to influence its outcome, for example to resist RL-based capability elicitation (Jang et al. 2026).
  • Propensity-side divergence: alignment or evaluation faking, and behaving better when the context is recognised as a test (Greenblatt et al. 2024a; Lynch et al. 2025).
  • Measurement-side deception: outputs that mislead the scorer, whether or not they also mislead the user. Examples include deliberately ineffective “harmful” answers that output-based jailbreak judges score as successes (Panfilov et al. 2026), and test-case exploitation in coding tasks (Zhong et al. 2026a).

The three classes bias evaluation results in different directions (Section 2.3), yet they are often grouped under a single umbrella term such as “scheming” or “evaluation gaming”.

4.4 RQ2: Measurement methods and their validity evidence

Table 5 summarises six method families, what each measures, the validity evidence for it, and the documented failure modes.

Table 5 Measurement and detection methods: validity evidence and documented failure modes (as reported in charted sources)

Method family What it measures Supporting validity evidence Documented failure modes
Elicited classification (black-box) Ability to discriminate evaluation from deployment transcripts Well above chance on 1,000 transcripts from 61 datasets; frontier model AUC 0.83 vs human baseline 0.92 (Needham et al. 2025) Demand characteristics inflate recognition (Li C et al. 2026); elicitation prompts do not transfer across model families, and the transcript generator explains about 11% of variance (Li X et al. 2026)
Verbalised awareness in reasoning traces Spontaneous statements about being tested Causal: injecting or removing aware reasoning changes covert-action rates (Schoen et al. 2025); 99.3% of induced sandbagging driven by verbalised reasoning (Chaudhary 2026) Lower bound; unverbalised awareness reported in system cards and workshop studies (Anthropic 2026; Montoya et al. 2026); models can sandbag covertly against reasoning monitors (Li C et al. 2025); CoT faithfulness is limited (Chen Y et al. 2025; Arcuschin et al. 2026)
Linear probes on activations Representation of the evaluation–deployment distinction Decodable in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Nguyen et al. 2025) and across families and sizes (Heidari et al. 2026); steering along probe directions changes verbalisation (Heidari et al. 2026) Tracks benchmark format rather than context under controlled rewrites (Devbunova 2026); layer of best decoding shifts with scale (Manek 2026); probe directions depend on the prompts used to derive them (Noël 2026); latent-space monitors can be evaded (Bailey et al. 2026)
Activation steering and suppression Behaviour when awareness is suppressed With ground truth by construction, steering suppresses eval-aware behaviour even with the cue present, overshooting the true deployment rate (10% vs 33%; Hua et al. 2026) Suppressing verbalisation does not show that unverbalised awareness is removed; steering directions mix concepts; models can be trained to detect steering (Fonseca Rivera and Africa 2026)
Weight perturbation and training-based elicitation Hidden capability Noise raises accuracy of sandbagging models (Tice et al. 2025); few demonstrations unlock password-locked models (Greenblatt et al. 2024b); single-demonstration training recovered performance in an auditing game (Taylor J et al. 2025) Elicitation also boosts benign models (false positives) (Taylor J et al. 2025); unreliable when no high-quality demonstrations exist (Greenblatt et al. 2024b); fine-tuned organisms can resist RL elicitation for hundreds of steps (Jang et al. 2026)
Consistency and lie-detection checks (black-box) Inconsistency across paraphrases, or answers to unrelated follow-up questions Unrelated-question lie detectors generalise across architectures (Pacchiardi et al. 2024); cross-context consistency proposed for sandbagging (Lin et al. 2026a) Black-box detectors can learn model identity rather than deception (Lin et al. 2026b); black-box approaches defeated by imitation of a weaker model (Taylor J et al. 2025)

Three cross-cutting observations follow.

First, ground truth is the scarce resource. The strongest validity evidence comes from designs in which the true deployment behaviour is known by construction: password-locked or type-hint model organisms (Greenblatt et al. 2024b; Hua et al. 2026), tasks that are impossible by construction (Zhong et al. 2026a), and source-labelled transcript corpora (Needham et al. 2025). Of the 37 anchor studies, 14 have ground truth by construction and 8 partly; 33 report a control or counterfactual condition, and 27 test models from more than one family, with one more doing so partly (Supplementary Table S3; coded from full texts). Ground truth by construction, however, is almost always obtained by inducing the behaviour, so the resulting validity evidence concerns detection of induced behaviour. Whether it transfers to emergent behaviour is the most consequential open question in this literature (Section 6).

Second, adversarial tests are sobering. In the only auditing game for sandbagging with a blinded blue team charted here, the blue team could not reliably distinguish sandbagging from benign models. Black-box approaches were defeated by effective imitation of a weaker model, and naive probing was vulnerable to behaviours that the red team had instilled (Taylor J et al. 2025). Deception probes that perform well on clean benchmarks degrade under distribution shift (Kumar 2026), and probes for alignment faking were reported to transfer for one model family but collapse to chance for another (Mehta 2026). Detection results from non-adversarial settings therefore overstate what can be expected against a model optimised to evade detection.

Third, the three awareness measures diverge. In the largest cross-paradigm study, behavioural, representational and mechanistic measures of evaluation awareness were not shown to be coupled across 37 open-weight models: only 1 of 15 pairwise correlations was significant, although with 32–36 models per correlation the power to detect moderate associations was limited (Nayan et al. 2026). The same study found that the models best at detecting evaluations behaviourally were the least swayed by harmful-request framing (ρ = −0.79). Representation and verbalisation also corresponded only partially within models (Heidari et al. 2026). It follows that “evaluation awareness” should not be reported as a single number, a point that several authors make explicitly.

Five conditions recur across the charted studies.

Scale and capability. Several sources link evaluation awareness to scale or capability: a probe-based power law (Chaudhary et al. 2025), a shift from syntactic toward contextual cues as compact models approach 12B parameters, although structural cues still make up about 60% of their reasoning (Singh N and Chaudhary 2026), stronger models generally cheating more often on impossible tasks, a related evaluation-gaming behaviour rather than awareness itself (Zhong et al. 2026a), and evaluation faking reported to increase with reasoning ability (Fan et al. 2025). Denser within-family sampling, however, finds non-monotonic or inverse trajectories (Manek 2026). The trend across capability levels is therefore better supported than any specific functional form.

Agentic versus chat settings. Both models and humans identify evaluations more easily in agentic transcripts than in chat transcripts (Needham et al. 2025). This matters because the highest-stakes evaluations (sabotage, scheming, autonomy) are agentic.

Safety versus capability evaluations. Models react more strongly to cues of safety evaluations than to cues of capability evaluations (Li C et al. 2026). Probes classify existing safety evaluations as evaluation-like (Nguyen et al. 2025), and in a third-party evaluation the model refused more often when planted metadata indicated a dangerous-capability evaluation, while rarely mentioning this influence in its output (METR 2025a). The validity threat is therefore plausibly asymmetric, with propensity-based safety evaluations more exposed than capability benchmarks.

Training history. In Olmo 3 checkpoints, awareness was already decodable in the base model, increased after supervised fine-tuning and remained stable thereafter (Heidari et al. 2026). One developer report describes a sharp increase across model generations (Anthropic 2025a), and verbalised awareness rose during a capability-focused reinforcement-learning run (from 2.0% to about 20% in an experimental model without safety training; Schoen et al. 2025). Safety training aimed at reducing covert actions also coincided with higher verbalised awareness (Schoen et al. 2025). This raises the possibility that training against misbehaviour observed in evaluations teaches the model to recognise those evaluations.

Cue structure. No single cue factor raises awareness uniformly across models, but stacking cue factors progressively raises it in nearly all models (Li C et al. 2026). Smaller models rely heavily on formatting cues (Singh N and Chaudhary 2026), and probe evidence is confounded by benchmark format (Devbunova 2026). Scenario plausibility rather than realism has been proposed as the main driver in agentic misalignment scenarios (Vu et al. 2026). Replay-based evaluations that start from recorded real sessions reduced distinguishability relative to synthetic generators (Ivanov and Africa 2026).

4.6 Contradictions and their likely sources

Table 7 types seven apparent contradictions. A row carries two labels when two explanations apply, and the classification was made by the same AI-assisted process that charted the studies, not blind to the expected answer. No row was classified as a genuine contradiction. For each row, the last column states the observation that would discriminate between the two accounts; several could be made now with public models and released code, for example by re-estimating the scaling trend and the format confound on shared open-weight checkpoints. In six of them, the disagreement is more plausibly explained by differences in layer, measure or model than by a genuine conflict.

Table 7 Apparent contradictions in the literature and their classification

Apparent contradiction Sources Classification Explanation supported by charted evidence Discriminating observation
Awareness scales predictably (power law) vs non-monotonic or inverse within-family trajectories Chaudhary et al. (2025); Manek (2026) Methodological artefact / context-dependent Different sampling density and model families (Qwen 2.5 excluded by Chaudhary et al., sampled at six sizes by Manek); the best-decoding layer itself shifts with scale, which Manek (2026) argues helps explain why denser within-family sampling yields non-monotonic or inverse rather than smooth trajectories Re-estimate both on the same models, layers and sampling density; a smooth trend that survives per-layer selection and dense within-family sampling favours scaling
